{"id": "36:12/q11", "question": "What are people's آثار?", "turns_on": "Whether the traces are literal tracks, continuing social effects, wealth, deeds as opposed to intentions, or specifically a legacy of error.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q11/p1", "position": "Good or evil legacies, practices, and consequences that continue after death.", "reasons": "Muqatil and the Prophetic precedent reports say originators share followers' reward or burden without reduction. Examples across al-Kashshaf, al-Qurtubi, al-Razi, al-Baydawi, al-Nasafi, al-Alusi, Elmalılı and Kuran Yolu include knowledge, books, charity, endowments, mosques, bridges, buildings, harmful policies, debased coinage, falsehood and corruption. Al-Mawardi includes later repair or corruption through one's character; al-Zajjaj prefers this broad common sense; al-Baghawi is said to choose it."}, {"id": "36:12/q11/p2", "position": "Footsteps or tracks, especially steps to mosques and Friday prayer.", "reasons": "Mujahid, al-Hasan, Qatada and others gloss آثار literally. Masruq says every step counts good or evil; Qatada and Umar b. Abd al-Aziz stress even wind-erased tracks. Anas specifies Friday. Al-Nahhas prefers footsteps from the Ansar occasion; Ibn Kathir says footsteps also imply lasting examples by stronger reasoning. Al-Alusi treats these as one included kind."}, {"id": "36:12/q11/p3", "position": "Misguidance specifically left as a legacy.", "reasons": "Mujahid's variant distinguishes good works sent ahead from error left behind; later sources transmit it."}, {"id": "36:12/q11/p4", "position": "Their deeds themselves, when ما قدموا is taken as intentions.", "reasons": "Al-Razi reports this pairing; Tabatabai rejects it in context."}, {"id": "36:12/q11/p5", "position": "Wealth left behind.", "reasons": "Abu Muslim gives this distinct explanation in Jishumi."}, {"id": "36:12/q11/p6", "position": "Every former deed, good or evil.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbi makes the traces encompass all prior works."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q12", "question": "What is the singular and vocalization of آثار?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q12/p1", "position": "Its singular is أثر, also pronounced إثر or with another athar vocalization.", "reasons": "Al-Nahhas and al-Qurtubi record the forms."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q13", "question": "How is ونكتب ... وآثارهم read?", "turns_on": "Active and accusative object coordination versus passive morphology and nominative deputy-subject analysis.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q13/p1", "position": "A passive reading has يُكْتَبُ or ويكتب and nominative آثارهم.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhshari notes passive yuktab and nominative kull; Ibn al-Jawzi attributes the passive and rafʿ of آثار to al-Nakhaʿi and al-Jahdari, while Abu Hayyan, al-Samin and al-Alusi cite Zirr and Masruq. Al-Samin makes آثارهم a deputy subject coordinated with ما قدموا; Ibn Atiyya separately attributes nominative آثارهم to Masruq."}, {"id": "36:12/q13/p2", "position": "The common active reading makes ما قدموا the object and آثارهم accusative by coordination.", "reasons": "Al-Samin describes the common construction; Ibn Atiyya notes a group with accusative آثارهم."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q14", "question": "What happened when a distant group considered moving near the mosque?", "turns_on": "Which group the report names and whether the episode is tied to revelation.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q14/p1", "position": "Banū Salima or the distant Ansar considered moving; the Prophet urged them to stay because their footsteps were recorded.", "reasons": "Reports vary in whether they complained, proposed selling homes, or received a prophetic response after the verse. Ibn Atiyya says the Prophet also disliked depopulating Medina. Jabir's version is in Muslim; Abu Saʿid's is graded hasan gharīb or hasan by al-Tirmidhi and authenticated by al-Hakim in later citations. Anas, Ibn Abbas, Abd Allah and al-Hasan supply variants."}, {"id": "36:12/q14/p2", "position": "Banū ʿUdhra, whose distant homes made prayer attendance hard, occasioned the verse.", "reasons": "Al-Mughira and al-Dahhak name Banu Udhra in al-Thaʿlabi; Jishumi gives the same name and footstep explanation."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q15", "question": "Was the verse newly revealed for the mosque relocation?", "turns_on": "Whether descent reports outweigh the Meccan setting, the Sahihayn recitation account, and the passage context.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q15/p1", "position": "Yes: reports say it descended when Banū Salima or the distant Ansar contemplated moving.", "reasons": "Abu Saʿid, Ibn Abbas and others explicitly use revelation language; a group makes this a Medinan exception to otherwise Meccan Yā Sīn. Al-Alusi argues the reports plainly say revelation then and rejects al-Khafaji's counterargument from the Sahihayn recitation."}, {"id": "36:12/q15/p2", "position": "No: the verse was Meccan and later invoked or recited in Medina.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya rejects the occasion because Yā Sīn was revealed in Mecca; Ibn Kathir finds a Medinan revelation strange; Abu Hayyan calls it unsound; al-Khafaji and Kuran Yolu point to the Sahihayn report in which the Prophet recites an already known verse. Tabatabai says the proposed occasion disrupts the passage's unified flow."}, {"id": "36:12/q15/p3", "position": "The wording is general, beyond Banū ʿUdhra or any one occasion.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports this response to his Banu Udhra account."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q16", "question": "What do the footstep reports teach about walking to prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q16/p1", "position": "Steps to and from prayer are individually recorded and rewarded, with greater distance bringing greater reward.", "reasons": "Uqba's report assigns a good deed and erased sin per step in both directions; Zayd cautions Anas against hurrying; Abu Musa's far-walker report occurs in Bukhari and Muslim; Ubayy's distant worshipper sought full credit rather than a donkey. Anas specifies Friday footsteps; Masruq and Qatada extend registration to good and bad steps, even wind-erased tracks. One report measures a migrant's distance from birthplace as reward in Paradise."}, {"id": "36:12/q16/p2", "position": "Waiting for the imam after walking earns additional reward.", "reasons": "The Prophet's report cited by al-Baghawi says waiting for prayer exceeds praying then sleeping."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q17", "question": "May one pass a local mosque for a farther one?", "turns_on": "Whether extra walking reward warrants passing one's own nearby mosque.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q17/p1", "position": "A farther mosque can yield greater reward.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi cites the footstep reports and Anas passing a new mosque for an old one; an Ibn Majah report gives one reward at home, twenty-five in a tribal mosque and five hundred in a congregational mosque."}, {"id": "36:12/q17/p2", "position": "One should not leave a nearby mosque merely for distance.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan and others disapprove, and al-Qurtubi identifies this with Malik's view; he reports juristic disagreement over passing the local mosque for the principal mosque."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q18", "question": "How are 'your homes' and 'we record' parsed in the mosque report?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q18/p1", "position": "Diyārakum is accusative exhortation to remain at home; naktub is jussive as the command's response.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi parses the words of the cited prophetic report."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q19", "question": "What other scripture explains deeds sent ahead and traces left behind?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q19/p1", "position": "75:13 and 82:5 give the parallel pair of what one sends ahead and leaves behind.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Ibn Qutayba, Yahya and later commentators make the comparison; al-Qurtubi also cites 59:18, and Study Quran cites 5:80. Ibn Kathir adds 17:71, 39:69 and 18:49 for complete personal records; Tabatabai cites 45:29 for truthful book testimony."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q20", "question": "What does كل شيء encompass?", "turns_on": "Whether كل شيء is unrestricted or bounded by the finite material capacity assigned to the Tablet.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q20/p1", "position": "Absolutely everything, extending beyond human works.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says past and future; al-Biqaʿi includes created and uncreated matters in eternal knowledge and writing; Bursawi includes human and nonhuman things; al-Razi says no word or act escapes, citing 54:52–53. Al-Alusi treats the universal as broad and considers Paradise's unending events separately."}, {"id": "36:12/q20/p2", "position": "All events in this world or through the Resurrection, a finite span.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi prefers a finite through-Judgment span for what the Tablet contains, restricting broad reports by narrower ones; others argue a finite physical Tablet cannot simultaneously inscribe infinite future events. Tabatabai calls this restriction arbitrary."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q21", "question": "How is وكل شيء أحصيناه parsed and read?", "turns_on": "Accusative through an implied or resumptive verb versus nominative as a new sentence.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q21/p1", "position": "Kull is accusative in an object-resumption or اشتغال construction.", "reasons": "Al-Farra says all readers choose accusative because the verb acts on its resumptive pronoun; al-Wahidi preserves his analogy to an earlier governing verb. Ibn Atiyya, al-Tabrisi, Bursawi and al-Alusi posit an understood verb explained by أحصيناه. Al-Nahhas, al-Khalil, Sibawayh and al-Samin prefer accusative, especially as it coordinates with prior verbal clauses."}, {"id": "36:12/q21/p2", "position": "Kull can be nominative as a fresh subject, with أحصيناه its predicate.", "reasons": "Al-Farra says the negative sense makes kull resemble an indefinite: nothing escaped. Abu al-Sammal, Ibn al-Sumayfiʿ and Ibn Abi Abla are cited for nominative; al-Wahidi calls it a new sentence."}]}

{"id": "36:12/q24", "question": "What is an إمام in language?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q24/p1", "position": "Something followed or guiding, whether person, book, or road.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjaj ties imam to intention and imitation; Ibn Qutayba says a road guides travelers. {"id": "36:12/q25", "question": "What is the clear إمام here?", "turns_on": "Whether Imam is the universal Tablet, deed-books, divine knowledge, a guiding book or path, or Ali in inner interpretation.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q25/p1", "position": "The Preserved Tablet or Mother of the Book, the comprehensive divine register.", "reasons": "Sources equate the two titles; al-Tabari says it records past and future; al-Wahidi says angels compare events to it; Tabatabai calls it the unchanged detailed decree and source of deed books; al-Alusi prefers it through Judgment, while avoiding claims about its substance. {"id": "36:12/q26", "question": "Why is the register called an إمام?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q26/p1", "position": "It is followed as guide, model, command, or authoritative proof.", "reasons": "Jishumi says angels follow the book or it precedes other books; al-Razi says angels follow instructions for lifespan, provision, life and death; Tabatabai says creation follows its inexorable decree and deed-books are copied from it; al-Nasafi calls it the model for other books."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q27", "question": "What makes the register مبين?", "turns_on": "Whether مبين qualifies a written register's legibility and testimony or knowledge's disclosure.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q27/p1", "position": "It makes what it contains plain or reveals the truth of recorded matters.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari says it reveals the record's truth; al-Razi says it shows angels their work, people their fate, and separates Paradise from Fire; al-Alusi says it manifests past and future. {"id": "36:12/q28", "question": "How can a finite Tablet contain everything?", "turns_on": "Whether the Tablet is a finite body, whether everything includes an infinite future, and whether writing may occur successively.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q28/p1", "position": "Limit the total record to worldly events or events through Resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi prefers the finite through-Judgment reading, reconciling unrestricted reports with restricted ones; Tabatabai reports the finite-body argument and rejects the limitation as arbitrary."}, {"id": "36:12/q28/p2", "position": "The Tablet's actual nature is unknown, so physical-capacity claims are insecure.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi avoids specifying its substance and does not accept ruby-and-emerald reports as certainly authentic; Tabatabai calls restriction arbitrary."}, {"id": "36:12/q28/p3", "position": "Successive installments could be inscribed, like the higher account in the Jafr al-Jamiʿ.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi proposes this if endless Paradise events are included."}, {"id": "36:12/q28/p4", "position": "Completed thousand-year sets could be erased and replaced.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi offers this further solution under the assumption of a finite physical Tablet."}]}
{"id": "36:12/q29", "question": "Are the deed-books and clear Imam one record?", "turns_on": "Whether two different registers are specified by the two clauses.", "positions": [{"id": "36:12/q29/p1", "position": "They are distinct: angelic personal books record deeds, while the Imam enumerates universal decree.", "reasons": "Tabatabai cites 6:59, 45:28 and 17:13 for universal, communal and personal registers, and says the verse contrasts writing with enumeration. Elmalılı likewise distinguishes prior Tablet inscription from later action recording."}, {"id": "36:12/q29/p2", "position": "Writing and enumeration describe the same encompassing divine record.", "reasons": "Al-Razi's preservation and generalization explanations and al-Biqaʿi's mutually implying writing and enumeration allow the expressions to converge; Tabatabai argues against this identification."}]}

{"id": "36:39/q01", "question": "What does qamar name here?", "turns_on": "Whether the verse follows restricted lexical usage or the familiar name of the celestial body.", "positions": [{"id": "36:39/q01/p1", "position": "The familiar moon throughout its monthly course.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī prefers this ordinary sense because the moon is paired with the sun; al-Qurṭubī connects the name to its brightness whitening the sky."}, {"id": "36:39/q01/p2", "position": "Strict lexical usage calls it qamar chiefly from about the third through twenty-sixth night, and hilāl near conjunction.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī attributes the distinction to lexicographers."}]}
{"id": "36:39/q02", "question": "How is wa-l-qamar read and construed?", "turns_on": "The recited case ending and whether the preceding nominal signs or the surrounding verbs govern the construction.", "positions": [{"id": "36:39/q02/p1", "position": "Nominative: the moon begins a nominal clause or is another sign alongside the night and sun.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, and in later lists Rawḥ/Yaʿqūb, Abū Jaʿfar, Ibn Muḥayṣin, al-Ḥasan, al-Aʿraj or Sahl are reported, with transmission variants for al-Ḥasan. The subject may have qaddarnāhu as predicate, or an implied āyatun lahum precedes it, with an understood predicate 'visible/existing' and ensuing explanatory clauses; al-Fārisī compares 36:37, 5:9, 4:11. Al-Farrāʾ, al-Naḥḥās and Abū Ḥātim prefer the nominal connection to earlier signs; Abū Ḥātim says the verb already bears an object pronoun. Al-Samīn says the nominal opening of wa-l-shams tajrī licenses it and judges both cases sound."}, {"id": "36:39/q02/p2", "position": "Accusative: the moon is a fronted object governed by an implied verb explained by qaddarnāhu, or is attached to an earlier verbal construction.", "reasons": "Kufans, Ibn ʿĀmir and other readers are reported. Al-Zajjāj supplies 'We appointed'; Sībawayh and al-Fārisī compare Zaydan ḍarabtuhu and allow linkage to naslakh. Abū ʿUbayd prefers accusative because verbs flank it; al-Ālūsī says the shift emphasizes divine determination and lunar month reckoning; al-Biqāʿī sees grandeur and speed, a month's travel matching the sun's year. Al-Samīn rejects al-Akhfash's condition of a pronoun referring to the sun: four readers and 55:5,7 counter it. Al-Samīn treats both cases as sound, following the verbal ending of wa-l-shams tajrī."}]}
{"id": "36:39/q03", "question": "How is the rāʾ of qaddarnāhu read?", "turns_on": "The transmitted vowel of the rāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "36:39/q03/p1", "position": "With ḍamma on the rāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr and Rawḥ transmit it."}, {"id": "36:39/q03/p2", "position": "With fatḥa on the rāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jazarī assigns it to the other readers."}]}
{"id": "36:39/q04", "question": "What did God measure or appoint?", "turns_on": "Whether the implicit object of determination is the course, the light, or the moon itself.", "positions": [{"id": "36:39/q04/p1", "position": "God appointed the moon's course and stations.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī gives course or course through stages; al-Ālūsī and Abū Ḥayyān understand the moon's path or place of travel; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī speaks of ordained stations; al-Burhān supplies 'for it.'"}, {"id": "36:39/q04/p2", "position": "God measured its light, which grows and diminishes.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī gives light as one possible omitted object; Abū Ḥayyān includes it; al-Ālūsī reports an explanation from changing sun-derived illumination and possible Earth eclipse, judging it more probable but uncertain."}, {"id": "36:39/q04/p3", "position": "God determined the moon itself through appointed stations or phases.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī permits direct determination; the ordinary explanation follows the moon through its changing monthly forms."}]}
{"id": "36:39/q05", "question": "How does manāzil function grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether manāzil is an object, an understood prepositional phrase, or a locative, especially given its bounded place sense.", "positions": [{"id": "36:39/q05/p1", "position": "It is a second object or an omitted 'possessor of stations' construction.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī supply dhā; al-Ṭabrisī says the omitted possessed noun leaves manāzil in its place, since the moon itself is not stations. Al-Samīn allows a second object if qaddara means 'made,' or a circumstantial dhā manāzil. Al-Ālūsī supplies the moon's course as first object; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī finds the 'possessing stations' sense clearest."}, {"id": "36:39/q05/p2", "position": "It stands for 'stations for it,' with an omitted preposition.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī compare omitted prepositions in 12:82 and 7:155; Abū al-Suʿūd prefers this parse as al-Ālūsī reports; al-Burhān also supplies 'for it.'"}, {"id": "36:39/q05/p3", "position": "It is an adverbial expression for the moon's course through stations.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn allow the parse. {"id": "36:39/q06", "question": "What are the moon's manāzil?", "turns_on": "The counting convention: the Arab twenty-eight visible stations versus the Indian astronomers' rounding of the sidereal period.", "positions": [{"id": "36:39/q06/p1", "position": "Twenty-eight named lunar stopping places or stellar markers.", "reasons": "Kuran Yolu explains manzil as a stopping place. Al-Sharaṭān: two bright Aries horn stars and a small neighbor, called al-Nātiḥ; its setting signaled rain and wind. Al-Buṭayn: three faint Aries thigh stars in a triangle. Al-Thurayyā: a six-star fan/grape cluster, with four Taurus-rump/Aries-tail stars noted; a cited poetic comparison has uncertain attribution to Aḥīḥah or Qays. Al-Dabarān: red Taurus eye after Pleiades, also Mijdah, amid eye, face and muzzle stars. Al-Haqʿa: three faint Orion-head dots, also Athāfī; al-Hanʿa: Orion shoulder or horse-neck brand, two stars; al-Dhirāʿ: two bright stars over Gemini, Lion's outstretched arm, against folded arm Sirius. Al-Nathra: Lion-nose gap, two faint stars and Cancer cloud patch, between the donkey stars; al-Ṭarf: two stars before Lion's eyes and paw; al-Jabha: four bent Lion-forehead stars, including bright Heart of the Lion; al-Zubra: two bright Lion mane/shoulder/nape stars; al-Ṣarfa: single Lion-tail star marking cold's turning; al-ʿAwwā: five bent Virgo stars, explained as howling dogs, cold-chaser, or bent shape, alternatively a person's lower part or Lion's hip. Al-Zubānā: two Libra-shoulder stars, or Scorpion horns. Al-Iklīl: three or four Scorpion-head stars like a crown; al-Qalb: bright red Scorpio-heart star with Niyāṭayn; al-Shawla: two bright Scorpion-tail stars; al-Naʿāʾim: Archer stars by the Milky Way, incoming and departing fours, likened to well beams; al-Balda: empty Archer sky patch like a den/desert/brow gap. {"id": "36:39/q08", "question": "How were the lunar stations used for seasons and weather?", "turns_on": "The observed stellar spacing and whether dawn visibility follows a fixed fourteen/fourteen division.", "positions": [{"id": "36:39/q08/p1", "position": "They marked the solar year, seasonal work and the rising and setting periods called anwāʾ.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba notes Arab linkage to rain omens. {"id": "36:39/q22", "question": "What do rain attributions to mansions imply?", "turns_on": "Whether the speaker assigns independent agency to stars or speaks of a cause under God's decree.", "positions": [{"id": "36:39/q22/p1", "position": "Believing the star itself sends rain is disbelief or apostasy.", "reasons": "Al-Shāfiʿī and others say an unrepentant speaker may be executed; al-Ālūsī cites al-Rawḍa for apostasy when true agency is assigned to a mansion."}, {"id": "36:39/q22/p2", "position": "Calling a mansion a divinely decreed cause is permitted, though some call the phrase ingratitude.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī calls permissibility the sound view when God remains the true agent; Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr regards even that phrase as ingratitude and ignorance of divine wisdom."}]}
